conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, and it helps us spot anything from the “baby blues” to postpartum depression or anxiety so we can support you better.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team—no judgment, just care. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. When you’re ready, we can begin.

First, thinking about this past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I guess I can still laugh sometimes… but honestly, it feels like work. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I managed a chuckle, yet it faded fast. Things that used to crack me up just feel kind of “meh” now—like the joy gets snuffed out before it really lands.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wouldn’t go that far… It’s more like I *can* laugh, but it doesn’t come easily. I have to remind myself to lighten up, and even when I do laugh, it feels kind of flat—like the happy feeling doesn’t last.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I *want* to look forward to stuff—like my mom keeps saying we should take the baby to the park or meet friends for coffee—but when the time comes, I just feel… blah. Even little things I used to enjoy, like my favorite show or a walk, feel more like chores than something nice ahead.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah… like if the baby won’t settle, I’ll catch myself thinking I must be doing something wrong or missing some “mom instinct” everyone else has. Last night he cried for almost an hour and I kept replaying everything—maybe I didn’t burp him right, maybe I ate something that bothered him. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the little voice in my head still says, “You should’ve figured it out by now.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly at night, after I put him in the bassinet. My mind just races—what if he spits up and I don’t hear him, what if his breathing sounds weird, what if I fall asleep too hard and don’t notice something’s wrong. There’s no real reason; the pediatrician says he’s perfectly healthy. But the worry shows up anyway and I lie there staring at the monitor, heart pounding, unable to settle even when he’s sleeping soundly.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times. Once, I was just folding laundry while the baby napped and all of a sudden my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get a full breath. Nothing triggered it—no loud noise, no bad news—just this wave of “something awful is about to happen.” It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky and watching the baby monitor like I was waiting for danger I couldn’t even name.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can check things off. I’ll finally get the baby down and realize the sink’s full of bottles, the diapers need ordering, and I haven’t eaten a real meal since breakfast. I’ll stand in the kitchen and think, “How am I supposed to keep all these plates spinning?” I manage, but by evening I’m exhausted and snapping at my partner over little stuff, then I feel guilty for losing my patience.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not so much that I’m lying there sobbing or anything… it’s more that my mind won’t hush. I’ll finally get the baby down around midnight, crawl into bed myself, and then every little worry queues up—did I sterilize the bottles right, is he gaining enough weight, did I forget to pay the pediatrician bill. I’ll drift off, but I’m up again at two-thirty, three, just staring at the ceiling, tense and wide-eyed even though I’m exhausted. By morning I feel like I’ve run a marathon I never signed up for.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel sad some days. It’s not constant, but it kind of creeps in—especially when the baby’s finally asleep and the house is quiet. I’ll look at him and feel this heaviness, like I should be overflowing with joy but instead I just feel empty or weepy. The other afternoon I was rocking him and started crying for no real reason. I wiped my face before anyone saw, but it scared me a little—like I don’t totally recognize myself right now.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not exactly... I’ve felt teary and low, but I usually manage to stop myself before the tears spill over. Once or twice this week my eyes filled up, but I blinked hard and distracted myself—checked the baby, folded a blanket, anything to keep from actually crying. I keep thinking if I let myself start, I might not be able to stop, so I hold it in.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that. My mind is mostly worried about keeping the baby safe and healthy; hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

Over the past week this new mother has felt as though joy is distant; laughter comes only with effort and quickly fades. She wakes at night flooded with worries about her healthy baby, experiences sudden heart-racing fear while doing routine tasks, and faces each day's small chores as if they were mountains. She describes a heavy, empty mood that surfaces unexpectedly, yet she gathers her strength to keep everything afloat, all while blaming herself for any hiccup along the way.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 20, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is effortful, fleeting, and joyless, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses near-complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, describing activities as "blah" and "chores," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame occurs "some of the time," matching option "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, nighttime-only worries that are intense and interfere with sleep, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly describes sudden onset panic-like symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, dread) without identifiable trigger, consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping with daily tasks, though still managing, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent sadness that intrudes unpredictably, leading to spontaneous crying, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 20 places her well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major <med>depressive</med> episode with peripartum onset. She endorses core symptoms: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), prominent self-reproach, daily anxiety, multiple panic-like episodes, and sleep disruption unrelated to infant care. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm ideation (Q10=0) reduces immediate safety risk but does not lessen clinical urgency. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> within one week
2. Request formal perinatal mental-health assessment and consider starting evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy</med> or <med>Interpersonal Therapy</med>
3. Discuss risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> if symptoms remain moderate-severe
4. Encourage 20-30 min daily outdoor walk or gentle exercise; enlist family to cover baby care during this time
5. Promote 4-hr max sleep stretch at night-partner/friend handles one feeding with pumped milk or formula
6. Provide 24-h7 helpline numbers (Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773, National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746)
7. Schedule EPDS re-screen in two weeks to monitor trend and intervention response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire, self-report, ~2–3 wk post-delivery.

Symptoms endorsed (mild–moderate intensity, present several days per week):
- Anhedonia / reduced pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (“missing mom instinct”; Q3)  
- Generalized & nocturnal anxiety, intrusive worries about infant safety (Q4)  
- Two episodes of sudden palpitations / dyspnea consistent with panic attacks (Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, irritable, unable to “keep plates spinning” (Q6)  
- Initial & middle insomnia linked to racing thoughts (Q7)  
- Sad / empty mood, tearfulness (Q8, Q9) – no full crying spells (suppressed)  

Safety screen: Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10). No psychotic or manic symptoms elicited.

Pattern: Meets screening cutoff for possible postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; no current safety concern.

Recommendation: Continue with formal EPDS scoring; consider referral for comprehensive perinatal mood assessment, psychoeducation, and support services.
